nameStory: This grass gets its "smooth" name from its hairless stems and leaves, which feel slick to the touch compared to its fuzzy relative, regular witchgrass. The "witch" part comes from an old English word meaning "bendable" or "flexible," referring to how the grass stems can bend without breaking in the wind.
description: Smooth witchgrass is an annual grass that grows in loose, spreading clumps from 1 to 4 feet tall. Its most striking feature is the open, airy seed head that branches out like a delicate cloud of tiny seeds in late summer and fall. The smooth, hairless stems are often reddish or purplish at the joints, and the whole plant has a somewhat sprawling growth habit that can form dense patches in disturbed areas.

idTips.label: Seed Head
idTips.description: Large, open, pyramid-shaped clusters of tiny seeds that feel papery and rustle softly in the breeze - much more open and airy than most other grasses

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Completely smooth and hairless stems that feel slick when you run your finger along them, often with reddish or purple coloring at the swollen joints

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, hairless leaves that are flat and about 1/4 to 1/2 inch wide with a prominent white midrib running down the center

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling, somewhat floppy annual grass that often leans or spreads outward rather than growing strictly upright, forming loose colonies

idTips.label: Timing
idTips.description: Seeds develop in late summer and fall, turning the whole plant into a conspicuous, golden-brown mass that persists into early winter

habitat: Look for smooth witchgrass in disturbed soils, vacant lots, roadsides, agricultural fields, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in sunny spots with rich, moist soil but can tolerate drought once established. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy grasses and annual plants in areas that have been recently disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small, bright green tufts with smooth leaves - easy to overlook among other emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and begin developing their characteristic open, branching seed heads in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: The large, airy seed heads become most prominent, turning golden-brown and highly visible as they tower over other vegetation. Seeds ripen and disperse.
seasonality.winter: Dead, dried stems and seed heads persist through early winter, appearing as bleached, papery skeletons until snow or strong winds break them down.

funFact: Each smooth witchgrass plant can produce over 50,000 seeds in a single season, and the seeds can remain viable in the soil for decades, waiting for the perfect conditions to sprout - which is why this grass seems to appear "magically" wherever soil gets disturbed.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with regular witchgrass, but smooth witchgrass lives up to its name - run your hand along the stem and it will feel completely smooth and slick, while regular witchgrass feels fuzzy and rough. Remember: smooth witchgrass = smooth feel.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "weed" by many gardeners, smooth witchgrass is actually a native plant that provides important food for wild birds and helps prevent soil erosion in disturbed areas. It's nature's way of quickly covering and protecting bare soil.
compareHints: Among the panicgrasses in New England, smooth witchgrass is the most sprawling and has the most open, airy seed head. Switchgrass grows much taller and more upright with denser clumps, while regular witchgrass is much fuzzier to the touch. The smooth, hairless stems and leaves combined with the loose, pyramid-shaped seed head make this species distinctive in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Switchgrass stands out from its panic grass relatives by its impressive size and clumping growth habit - most other Panicum species in New England are much smaller annual weeds.
Witch grass stands out from its Panicum relatives by its distinctive tumbleweed habit and proportionally enormous seed head.
Among its panicgrass relatives in New England, bitter panicgrass stands out as the giant of the family and the only one adapted to coastal life.
Unlike its wild native relatives like switchgrass and witch grass, proso millet has much larger, rounder seeds and broader leaves.
Among the panicgrasses, Philadelphia panic grass is the most delicate and smallest.

**Uncertain comparisons:** Compared to its relatives, Gattinger's panic grass is typically smaller and more delicate than switchgrass, less weedy-looking than witch grass, and has more open, airy flower clusters than the denser-flowered smooth witchgrass.
